value.overview: The White-winged Tanager (Piranga leucoptera) is a colorful forest tanager found from Mexico through Central America and in parts of northern and western South America. It is a medium-sized songbird of humid mountain forests, cloud forests, mature secondary growth, and shaded plantations. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon resident of the highland cordilleras, where it often travels alone, in pairs, or with mixed-species feeding flocks.
value.classification: The White-winged Tanager belongs to the cardinal family, Cardinalidae, in the genus Piranga. It is not closely related to many tanagers in the family Thraupidae.
value.identification: Adults are recognized by their bright yellow underparts, dark wings with two conspicuous white wing bars, and olive to gray-green upperparts. Adult males usually show a reddish head and upper breast, while females are more uniformly yellow below with a subdued olive head and back. Immature birds resemble females but are duller. The species has a fairly slim tanager shape and is often detected in the forest canopy or along woodland edges.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and southward into the Andes and adjacent lowlands of northern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a scarce to uncommon resident mainly in the upper parts of the northern cordilleras, the Caribbean side of the Central Volcanic Cordillera, and both slopes of the Talamanca Cordillera, including Dota and southern coastal ranges. It generally occurs at about 1,100–1,850 meters, in montane forest, cloud forest, mature secondary woodland, forest edges, and nearby shaded trees or coffee plantations.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a resident species in Costa Rica rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur with changes in food availability or elevation, but the Costa Rican population is present year-round in suitable highland habitats.
value.breeding: Breeding has been documented in Costa Rica, with nesting reported mainly from April to May. The female builds a small cup nest, including a documented nest placed high on a moss-covered branch about 14 meters above the ground. Detailed information on clutch size, eggs, incubation, and parental care remains limited. Breeding habitat includes montane forest and forest-associated trees in open or semi-open mountain areas.
value.dietFeeding: The White-winged Tanager feeds mainly on fruits, berries, and seeds, and it probably also takes insects and other small arthropods. It usually forages in the canopy or at forest edges, where it may search among foliage and branches. In Costa Rica, it commonly joins mixed-species flocks containing other tanagers, warblers, honeycreepers, and small forest birds.
value.behavior: Individuals are often solitary or found in pairs, although they regularly participate in mixed-species foraging flocks. The species is generally active in the upper and middle levels of humid mountain forest. Its thin, high-pitched song and varied calls can help reveal its presence, but the bird may remain difficult to see among dense canopy foliage. It is a mobile, alert forager that frequently moves between perches while searching for fruit and insects.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species has a broad distribution and is not currently considered globally threatened.
